findings.source_passage: Your woraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame ye so much for; dat is natur, and can't be helped; but to gobern dat wicked natur, dat is de pint.
findings.source_locator: Fleece's second sermon passage, beginning 'Your woraciousness'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft collapses the opening of the core sermon—'I don't blame ye so much for; dat is natur, and can't be helped'—into a paraphrase, losing the dialectal rhythm and the moral logic ('can't be helped' vs. the pint of governing) that critics return to as the chapter's philosophical center.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim opening of this speech: 'Your woraciousness, fellow-critters, I don't blame ye so much for; dat is natur, and can't be helped; but to gobern dat wicked natur, dat is de pint.'

findings.source_passage: "Well done, old Fleece!" cried Stubb, "that's Christianity; go on."
findings.source_locator: After Fleece's sermon on sharing the blubber fairly
findings.why_it_matters: Stubb's interjection 'that's Christianity; go on' is the interpretive keystone of the passage—it reframes a parody sermon as genuine moral commentary and is the line critics cite when discussing Melville's satire of Christian ethics in the chapter.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Stubb's exclamation verbatim after Fleece's 'dat whale belong to some one else' speech.

findings.source_passage: "dare bellies is bottomless; and when dey do get 'em full, dey wont hear you den; for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral"
findings.source_locator: Fleece's final despairing speech before the benediction
findings.why_it_matters: The draft replaces Fleece's full despairing peroration with a compressed summary; the rhythm and the image of sinking to sleep 'on de coral' for 'eber and eber' carry strong voice weight and are erased.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim passage: 'dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear not'ing at all, no more, for eber and eber.'

findings.source_passage: "When dis old brack man dies," said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and demeanor, "he hisself won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him."
findings.source_locator: The heaven dialogue, Fleece's response to 'when you die, cook'
findings.why_it_matters: The stage direction 'changing his whole air and demeanor' and Fleece's verbatim answer are interpretively significant—the sudden shift in register signals genuine dignity beneath the comic framing, a moment critics note as Melville's humanizing counter-pressure. The draft reduces this entire exchange to a brief paraphrase ('On heaven: Fleece pointed "up dere"').
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Fleece's answer verbatim including the narratorial 'changing his whole air and demeanor,' then include the fetch-Elijah exchange, and Stubb's lubber's-hole riff—at least in compressed but voice-faithful form.

findings.source_passage: 'Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin' ober de Roanoke... you must go home and be born over again; you don't know how to cook a whale-steak yet.
findings.source_locator: The birthplace cross-examination, middle of the Stubb–Fleece dialogue
findings.why_it_matters: The comic catechism on age and birthplace—culminating in Stubb's 'you must go home and be born over again'—is compressed to 'cross-questioned him on age and birthplace,' erasing Stubb's absurdist punchline and Fleece's Roanoke answer.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore at minimum: Fleece's 'Bout ninety' and Roanoke answers, and Stubb's 'you must go home and be born over again; you don't know how to cook a whale-steak yet.'

summary: The draft preserves the chapter's structure and several verbatim set-pieces well, but four medium-severity failures—erasure of 'that's Christianity; go on,' flattening of Fleece's despairing peroration, near-total loss of the death/heaven/dignity exchange, and compression of the 'born over again' punchline—collectively strip the chapter's interpretive and comic core, meeting the regenerate threshold.
